title: Burst recovery path analysis: proxy buffer oscillation impact on streaming SLOs
content:
Summary:
We ran a focused set of stress experiments to understand why short client bursts sometimes trigger multi-second tail latency spikes even when average CPU/GPU utilization looks fine. The main finding: certain proxy buffering/coalescing configurations create a feedback loop with client flush patterns that produces oscillatory egress behavior ("buffer oscillation") which amplifies backpressure and stalls KV-cache warmups. This is different from a single spike due to queueing — it manifests as repeated mini-spikes over ~5–30s after a burst.

Why this matters:
- Customers see intermittent 95th/99th token latency regressions despite similar median.
- Dedicated capacity SLOs are sensitive to sustained tail bands; repeated mini-spikes can push p99 beyond SLA windows.
- Mitigations at app-level (retries/timeouts) mask but do not fix the underlying oscillation.

Hypothesis and framing:
- Hypothesis: When many clients emit sub-100ms bursts, proxies with coalescing enabled hold small frames until either a timer fires or a coalesce threshold is reached. If upstream worker responses arrive in a rhythm (b/c of batching or KV-warmup), coalescing can align outgoing packet windows. This alignment causes transient queues at proxynodes -> proxy starts to apply egress pacing -> clients observe delayed flushes and then flush again, re-triggering the cycle.
- We define an "oscillation index" OI = stddev(1s-throughput-samples)/mean(1s-throughput-samples) measured over a 30s window as a simple proxy for burst oscillation severity.

Test matrix (concise):
- Workload: synthetic chat-like stream: 1–5 token increments, openai-compatible chunked gRPC streaming.
- Client patterns: (A) aligned bursts: 100 clients send 30 requests simultaneously every 60s; (B) jittered bursts: same but jitter +/- 200ms; (C) steady low: 500 rps steady with poisson interarrival.
- Proxy modes: (1) coalesce-on (timer 3ms, threshold 4 packets), (2) coalesce-off (immediate flush), (3) adaptive-drip (long-tail smoothing enabled), (4) large-send-buffer (increase SO_SNDBUF).
- Backend: 4 worker replicas (A100-like), KV-cache cold/warm variants. All runs repeated x5.

Environment notes (important for reproducing):
- K8s nodes: r5-machine-proxy-1..4 (Ubuntu 22.04), kernel 6.1, iptables disabled in favor of nft, net.core.default_qdisc=fq
- Proxy: internal edge-proxy v2.4.1 (build ref: sha256:abc123), compiled with grpc-http2 multiplexing support.
- Client harness: go-loadgen (proc), version commit: 6e4f9d; synchronized via NTP and splayed start times.

Observations / key numbers (representative):
- Aligned bursts + coalesce-on: p50 ~ 120ms, p95 ~ 430ms, p99 ~ 1.3s across 30s post-burst; OI median 0.42.
- Aligned bursts + coalesce-off: p50 ~ 110ms, p95 ~ 190ms, p99 ~ 260ms; OI median 0.09.
- Jittered bursts + coalesce-on: p95 ~ 210ms (better than aligned), OI median 0.18.
- Adaptive-drip reduced p99 by ~40% versus coalesce-on for aligned bursts, but increased median by ~10ms due to serialization.
- Large-send-buffer lowered immediate packetization overhead but had negligible effect on OI; it reduced packet-counts but did not break the rhythm.

Time-series notes (qualitative):
- When coalesce-on and clients aligned, we observe a clear oscillatory pattern in egress throughput: sharp dip 200–600ms after burst, then a rebound overshoot, repeating 3–8 times while KV-cache warms.
- Traces show many small responses queued at proxy egress; the queue drains in microbursts.
- gRPC-level RTTs reported by clients correspond to proxy drain windows rather than backend processing time.

Root cause analysis (short):
- Alignment + coalescing creates rhythmic batches of egress frames leading to bursty network transmit patterns. Backpressure signals (tcp window shrinkage / internal pacer) cascade back to worker threads and interact poorly with our worker’s prioritization of new requests vs. KV cache hits, causing slower token emission at steady state.
- The system is sensitive to deterministic coalesce timers + synchronized client behavior; adding jitter at the client or making proxy coalescing deterministic-break (randomized timers) reduces alignment.

Mitigations tested and recommended order:
1) Short-term: disable coalescing for paths with streaming chat where p99 matters (config flag per route). Effective but increases packet count and small CPU overhead on proxies.
2) Medium-term: make coalesce timer randomized within [1ms, 5ms] and lower threshold from 4 -> 2. Reduced OI by ~60% in aligned burst tests.
3) Long-term: implement rate smoothing at ingress combined with token-paced egress (adaptive-drip) that keeps steady small writes rather than microbursts. Works but introduces slight median latency regression; best for enterprise SLO targets.
4) Client mitigation: recommend client-side jitter and small random backoff on flushes when many parallel streams are in flight (doc sample in linked artifacts).

Operational guidance for rollout:
- Feature-flag randomized-timer behind a canary for 10% of prod traffic; monitor OI, p99, packet-rate.
- Enable route-level override for customers that rely on tight median latency (they may opt-out).
- Add an observability metric: proxy_egress_oscillation_index (1s samples) and alert when >0.25 for 30s.

Open questions / TODOs:
- TODO: repeat with QUIC/proxy path (we only tested http2/gRPC). Hypothesis: QUIC will reduce tail due to connection-level congestion control differences but may still show alignment if coalescing exists at app-level.
- TODO: quantify CPU cost increase for randomized coalescing at 10k rps cluster-wide.
- Open: how does TLS record coalescing interact with proxy buffers on middleboxes? Need to run with middlebox sim.

Raw artifacts and where to find data:
- Raw pcap + p95 traces: gs://redwood-infra/bench/burst-recovery-nov2026/ (see README there)
- Load harness config: github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/configs/burst-recovery-2026.yaml
- Jupyter dashboards: internal dashboards (link in linked_artifacts ticket)

Notes to self / meeting agenda items:
- Walk DevOps on rolling randomized-timer feature
- Discuss default route-level setting for coalescing
- Validate QUIC experiments with network team

Quick verdict (for PMs):
- Cause: proxy-induced alignment + coalescing creates oscillation that amplifies tail latency during bursts.
- Short-term fix: disable coalescing on streaming routes; Medium-term: randomized timer; Long-term: smoothing + token-pacing in runtime.

Unresolved observations (for follow-up):
- We observed one run where coalesce-off still had elevated p99 despite low OI — hypothesis: client-side retransmits caused replay congestion; need packet-level timeline correlation.

End of note.
